utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Good morning, Excellencies. [Interpretation] Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Clark. I don't know how much time we have left, but I'm going to do my best to finish in the time allotted to me. I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are we receiving the English translation? Oh, yes. Then please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about what we were talking about during our interview. You did not recall if there was any Serbian presence during the exhumations, during the work of the pathologists doing the autopsies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was no Serbian presence at all in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Judges do not get the English translations except for Judge Baird. Doctor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm getting it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Technicians will take a look. In the meantime, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, you used, to an extent, also the interviews and statements of witnesses when you were putting the whole picture together; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the translation through the headphones, but I'm reading it on the screen which will take a little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a break for five or ten minutes. --- Break taken at 9.05 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I hope everything has been sorted out. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Now I do not have anything in my ear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was: You -- when you were putting the whole picture together, you were also using interviews by the investigators with other persons, witnesses of sorts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. With one exception, these reports were compiled entirely from the post mortem reports together with a little bit of background information for the site which we had been given at the start of the procedure. The only exception was the four bodies from Vlasenica in which I was given detailed witness statements to consider, but other than that, absolutely nothing other than vague -- just general background information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is as far as what actually reached you, but others had different information. Do you know if any interviews were conducted with witnesses by, for example, investigators and those who were conducting the exhumations and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, undoubtedly the investigators would have carried out interviews; that was their role. That information did not reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. In your opinion, in view of the fact that this is a conflict between two sides, between two ethnic and religious communities, would it be fair for there to have been Serbian experts present there, at least for them to be able to have access if not to participate, especially when we're talking about exhumations and other investigative actions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have had no problem myself in having Serb pathologists present in the mortuary. That was not my decision. I'm aware, however, that Serb authorities have had a chance to look at all the post mortem reports and to comment on them and have done so. And I've seen -- I have seen some of their comments. But that was not my decision to take, whether to have Serb pathologists present. As I say, I would have had no problem at all in them attending, standing beside me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, of course I didn't think that any of those conducting the autopsies would have made this decision, but it was a fact that in Visoko all the bodies, both of the Muslim and Serb victims, were put away but the Muslim bodies were not accessible to the Serbian experts without permission of the Muslim side. You knew that, of course; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In a number of cases you found traces of gun-shot wounds from a shot-gun even though it could not be concluded that the cause of death was that weapon. However, the presence of gun-shot was established in a number of bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This was a small number of people in which we found typical shot-gun pellets, clearly indicating that a shot-gun had been used as opposed to a handgun or a high-velocity weapon. They were concentrated in I think -- I think Nova Kasaba and probably one of the other sites. I may have that wrong. But there was a fairly small number. At least some of these people also had high-velocity weapon injuries, but as I recall, in two cases the only injury we found was shot-gun injury and we attributed that as the cause of death. It wasn't a common finding, but it's -- certainly was present in occasional cases, shot-gun pellets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive information about the degree to which civilians were armed before the war broke out and as it was breaking out? Did you receive any information as to the extent to which the civilian population had various types of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not given any information specifically on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with my assertion that civilians easily could have had both an automatic rifle and a shot-gun while soldiers and policemen only had automatic rifles. They did not have shot-guns, at least it was not recorded anywhere as being part of the weaponry available to the armed formations.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it's possible that civilians had access to shot-guns. I can't say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that it would be unusual for the army or the police to have shot-guns --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, is that a question for this expert witness? Please move on to your next questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a number of cases in Zeleni Jadar, even in 7 per cent of the cases you found that -- you found blast injuries and the presence of shrapnel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we certainly found shrapnel. I'm just checking the percentage. I think it was actually seven cases. We found blast damage in seven men out of 101 bodies, yes, you're right, 7 per cent, it is the same. They had blast damage and pieces of shrapnel which were I have to say very similar to the shrapnel we found in Glogova, one of the graves in Glogova, which is the only other grave in which we did find shrapnel. So Glogova and Zeleni Jadar both had evidence of shrapnel injuries. No other graves had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive information at all that in the cases when trenches were captured by one or the other side, these same trenches were also used as places of burial, as graves, and the opponent's casualties would be buried in an existing grave. Did anybody inform you about that? Do you know if this was something that happened or if it was possible at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that this is an opening question relating to the presence of bullet casings. I think in a number of cases, perhaps in Kasaba and Konjevic Polje - but this was not in your report, it was in the report of those who actually conducted the exhumations - but in your findings it states that in a number of graves there were significant shell casings found. I just wanted to tell you that when a trench is captured, then that trench is used as a ready-made grave for enemy soldiers. So is it possible that the shells that were found in the trench or around the trench or around the grave could have originated from fire that was originating from that place, i.e., that in the fighting there was actually shooting from those places?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly could be one explanation for shell cases beside the bodies. It has to be said that we found shell casing in only a very few bodies. There was -- I think in Ravnice we found some, but it wasn't a common finding at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, these lines of questions do not help the Chamber, all speculative. I think it's now time for you to wrap up your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in some cases you saw traces of animal-caused damage, which would indicate that before burial the body was accessible to wild animals?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the only site we saw that was in Ravnice in which I understand the bodies were already -- well, found out in the open anyway on a slope. I'm not aware that we found animal damage in any of the other bodies. Bear in mind we were only looking at skeletons. Earlier animal damage would, of course, affect the skin, which wasn't present here. But apart from Ravnice we saw no evidence of animal damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we agree perhaps that DNA findings may be used only for identification, but certainly not to determine the cause of death, the time of death, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, entirely, yes. It is only for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitchell, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No, I don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Dr. Clark. That concludes your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague yet again to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell, please call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is Mr. Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, while we're waiting to bring in the next witness, I just wanted to ask the Chamber that we received a filing yesterday from the Registry in connection with Witness KDZ523 and part of that filing was ex parte. And it's our request that that ex parte portion of the filing be made available to the parties. I'd like you to consider that when dealing with that request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address the Court regarding the sequence of witnesses. Due to some mistake, I expected Mr. Kingori for today. Is it a problem to change the order of witnesses because I haven't brought the background material for Mr. Peccerelli. I would have to print it off the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you need for that preparation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll see what I can print off from here, but I've left all the background material for this witness back there. I was ready for Mr. Kingori. I'll see in a few minutes what I can access.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, would you have a problem if we begin with Mr. Kingori?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Peccerelli is flying out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- at 9.00 tomorrow morning, so he really needs to finish today if at all possible. And I believe Mr. Kingori is not here yet. He's not -- he's physically in The Hague, but he's not coming in until -- for at least another couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Peccerelli. Due to some administrative matters, probably the Chamber needs to break about at least half an hour and I hope with the assistance of the Registry I think that problem could be sorted out. We'll take a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to apologise, but I must inform you that my living and working conditions have deteriorated because the Registry, probably for saving purposes, put me in a wing where we are 17 or 18 instead of seven to eight and I can use only a public telephone. If I want to use the telephone in the office on the ground floor, I have to write a special request. And if there is nobody at the administration, then I can make the phone call only the day after. I have no way of contacting my team. Without any need whatsoever, so many of us are crammed into one wing, which makes the overall living conditions much worse. And certain restrictions are now imposed not related to the personnel but without any justification and that creates a lot of problems for me because I have no way of using a secure line because all my associates are only accessible on mobile phones. And the Registry allows secure communication only on land-lines. None of my associates are available on land-lines. That is why I am experiencing these difficulties and I want you to know that. During the recess I was placed into a different wing where we are very many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll note that, but I believe there are ways to address the matter. Very well. Would the witness kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise on behalf of the Chamber for your inconveniences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Would you please state and spell your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: My name is Fredy Peccerelli, F-r-e-d-y P-e-c-c-e-r-e-l-l-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Before we start can you describe what that material is that's in front of you at the moment?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yeah, I have a copy of the Lazete 1 report, the Lazete 2 report, as well as copies of the registry logs for both excavation and exhumation procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I am a forensic and biological anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter number 3454 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, this is a copy of your CV. We can see on the first page that you're the executive director of the Guatemalan Forensic Anthropology Foundation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your work there, what it is that you do.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I have been working for the Guatemalan Forensic Anthropology Foundation since 1995, 17 years now. I direct the full operations of the institution. These are mainly operational duties as well as public speaking and fund gathering for the organisation. I have grown -- or helped the organisation to grow from five individuals to currently 136 individuals. The organisation has four technical areas. These are forensic archaeology, forensic anthropology, forensic genetics, as well as the investigation of missing peoples -- missing persons unit. We have a multi-disciplinary approach to the search of missing persons, recovery of evidence, and we investigate the crimes of the Guatemalan internal armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You worked for the ICTY's Office of the Prosecutor in 1997, 1998, and 2000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What was your position in 1997 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, 1997 I was hired as a forensic archaeologist and in 1998 as a forensic anthropologist. My duties were documentation, recovery and exhumation of human remains from mass graves. In 1997 specifically from Brcko and in 1998 with sites associated with the Srebrenica killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In 2000 you worked as the deputy senior forensic archaeologist for the ICTY; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe what that role was, who you reported to and what your responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, I was called upon by Dr. -- Professor Richard Wright. He told me that he was going to be leaving to Australia because of some personal or academic reasons and he wanted me to take over while he was gone. So I was instructed to lead a team of international archaeologists and anthropologists in the recovery, exhumation, and documentation of mass graves. Specifically, I was instructed to exhume the grave of Lazete 1 initially and then later Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And did you write reports on those two exhumations at Lazete 1 and Lazete 2?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I rendered two reports. They're entitled "Lazete 1" and "Lazete 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to move to tender Mr. Peccerelli's CV. It was 65 ter 3454. The Lazete 1 report which is 65 ter 2482. And the Lazete 2 report which is 65 ter 11151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. They will all be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be Exhibits P4134 through to 4136 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, do you recall testifying about these two reports in the Tolimir case on the 6th of December, 2000 -- sorry, 2010?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, 2010, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review that testimony recently?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I've read the full testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, I understand there is one correction to make. At transcript page 8464, line 10 of that testimony, you state that there was a wire ligature around the leg of a body in the Lazete 1 grave. It's correct that that was actually a strip of pink material around the leg of that body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was, if I recall correctly, body 474, LZ B474, and it actually has a strip of pink scalloped material that's tied around the thighs of both legs and then also the lower leg of -- one of the lower legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: With that one correction can you confirm that that transcript accurately reflects your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It accurately represents my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions on the same topics today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender Mr. Peccerelli's Tolimir testimony. That's 65 ter 23511. And there was one associated exhibit that we have requested leave to add to our 65 ter list and tender. That's number 23513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you also need a leave to add this photo to your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President. We were -- request that leave in our notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That leave is granted and we'll admit the transcript in the Tolimir case as Exhibit P4137 in this case. And we'll give the number for that associated exhibit, Exhibit P4138.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to read a summary of Mr. Peccerelli's testimony from the Tolimir case. In 2000, Mr. Peccerelli oversaw the excavation and exhumation of two mass graves known as Lazete 1 and Lazete 2C. The Lazete 1 grave was a partially robbed primary grave that was exhumed between the 13th of July and the 8th of August, 2000. It measured 15.8 metres long, 5.8 metres wide and 1.4 metres deep. It contained 127 bodies in three distinct concentrations as well as two additional bodies that were found in an adjacent ditch. Ligatures were associated with the wrists of two bodies, while probable blindfolds were associated with 89 bodies. A further 37 pieces of material were located in the grave fill. These 37 items appear to be the same material from which the probable blindfolds were made. 456 shell casings were found grouped together on the southern edge of the Lazete 1 grave area, mostly on the side of a track leading into the field where the grave was located. Mr. Peccerelli testified that the grouping of the shell casings suggested that firing had occurred in that location. The Lazete 2C grave was a large primary grave that was excavated and exhumed by Mr. Peccerelli's team in August 2000. It was much larger than the Lazete 1 site, measuring 37.7 metres in length and 4 metres in width. The grave had been partially robbed in September 1995 and two sections of the grave designated as Lazete 2A and Lazete 2B had previously been excavated in 1996 by a team from Physicians from Human Rights, or PHR, led by Mr. Bill Haglund. From this grave Mr. Peccerelli's team recovered 16 bodies and 26 body parts that had not previously been removed either during the robbing event in September 1995 or PHR's partial exhumation in 1996. Probable blindfolds were associated with eight of these 16 bodies. 671 shell casings were found grouped together near the Lazete 2C grave. Mr. Peccerelli concluded that the shell casings were most likely fired at this location. In addition, 20 live rounds, 46 bullets, and 34 strips of material were found at the Lazete 2C site. The strips of material found at the Lazete 2C site were consistent with the strips of material found at the Lazete 1 mass grave site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, I have a few additional questions on three topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have 65 ter 2482 in e-court. It's Exhibit P4135.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is your report on Lazete 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can have page 12 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, I think that's page 11 in the hard copy of your report. Now, we can see here some photos of the site that you exhumed. Were you able to tell whether the bodies in the Lazete 1 grave were deposited in one event or were they deposited there at different times, possibly over a period of several years?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: During the excavation we were able to establish that a single event was the cause of this grave. The grave showed uniform profiles and as well as a uniform bottom. The bodies were displaced in a uniform manner and clumped together throughout the grave. And the only thing where we can see that there was a secondary excavation on the grave was when a robbing event occurred posterior to the primary grave being dug, and this was seen by a difference in the soil fill in those two robbing areas as well as the presence of truncated body parts -- truncated bodies as well as the creation of body parts specifically on the edges of the robbing areas as well as in the fill. It is important to note that throughout the grave you can see a continuum of the edges of the grave as well as of the equipment that was used to create this grave. And the bodies are laid on top of each other only with small pieces of top-soil among them. This indicates that the bodies were placed in there at one time and most likely had this top-soil among the bodies, between the bodies, because of the way they were placed in the grave, most likely pushed in the grave by machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What would you expect to see -- what archaeological evidence would you expect to see if the bodies had been placed in there at different times?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we would expect to see the existence of disarticulation of the bodies, which we did not see here. Even the body parts were articulated among the bones that were there, that were left. In other words, these were severed during an extraction process that was posterior to the initial burial and these showed the same type of decomposition as the rest of the bodies. We did not see any signs of features within the grave that would lead us to believe that this was a prior burial of any type. The hole, the original hole that later turned into a grave when the bodies were deposited into it was dug into a virgin clay yellowish soil and the fill was a combination of the strata that was exhumed as well as the top-soil that was deposited into it over the bodies and this was uniform throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: At page 21 of this report you describe how the 20 -- 129 bodies from this grave were found in various states of decomposition. So if these bodies all went into the grave in a single event, can you explain why the bodies show differential rates of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, well, I have worked in over 1400 investigations in Guatemala, and when it comes to mass graves there is differential decomposition due to many factors but decomposition in itself is a very complex issue. It is impacted by specifically three types of differences. For example, first we look at the biological aspects of decomposition, then we look at the environmental and then the cultural. As far as the biological, we have to remember that bodies might decompose differently due to their weight, their size, and their sex even. As far as environmental, we have to remember that the difference in humidity or acidity of the soil will also impact the bodies differently and how close these bodies are to that soil. Thirdly, as far as cultural aspects, well, in this case we're talking about a mass grave. The bodies were buried and also the cause of death or the trauma that was impacted on the bodies will also affect the decomposition. Specifically in this case the bodies that are closer to the edges or in contact, direct contact, with the soil or are higher in the surface of the grave will decompose at slightly faster rate. And the bodies that are in the nucleus of the grouping of bodies will be protected from the environment more so and will decompose slightly slower. Now, you do have to remember that the decomposition stages here are transient. In other words, there we're talking about advanced decomposition to skeletonisation. So there is no one step jumping to the other. This is a transient state and the bodies are all among those too. They show adipocere which is a greyish-whitish tissue, sort of greasy initially and then eventually it becomes brittle and eventually into skeletonisation. This is exactly what we have throughout these bodies in the entire grave. So the difference is very slight and it is related to the location of the bodies within the grave. Once again, the bodies that are protected from the environment by other bodies decompose at a slightly slower rate than the bodies that are in direct contact with the soil.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: After you had established that these bodies were placed in the grave in a single event, were you able to determine when this single event occurred?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, archaeologically we were not able to do so. What we did have was images that we were given by the ICTY investigators. Dean Manning I think was his name at the time. He gave me an image. I think it's the image that's on the screen now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we can bring up a larger version of that image. If we can have 65 ter 3199 and go to page 146 in e-court. It's the same image but bigger and better quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps if the usher can assist you, I might ask you to mark some things on this photo as you're describing to us what you can see. If you can go ahead with your explanation.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: When we were -- the team was given these images, we studied them. And what we could see, these are two images, aerial images, taken of the same location. And you can see that we are talking about basically this quadrant here which appears in this image as this quadrant there. And then we're also talking about this section here, which appears more or less there. You can see they are slightly different and this is probably because of the angles of where the pictures were taken, but in the one on my left, which is dated July 5th, you can see that on both fields there are no features that are relevant. In other words, there's nothing we can see. We can see homogenous ground, vegetation looks pretty much the same, these are cleared fields with maybe a slight feature going to the middle of the top one. But then on the one on the right that is dated July 27th, we can see that there are specifically an oval-shaped feature with tracks going around it and in the bottom one you can see also an oval-shaped feature with some spillover on both of these. Once we saw these images, what we believe we're seeing here is the result of turning the soil over, in other words, exposing soil that was underneath and breaking the top-soil, taking the vegetation away, and then covering it up again. So you would see this very differently from the surrounding vegetation. And also the shapes of the two features led us to believe that these could be graves. So we decided that we should excavate -- well, initially it was only Lazete 1, which is the one on top --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I stop you there for a minute. Can you actually mark on this image Lazete 1 -- LZ01.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Pen went over it. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then put in the -- for the lower site what its name is.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can see that. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Because of the two dates -- I mean, we requested images in between the dates, but we were told that they didn't have them. So we placed the dates of the original excavation of the primary grave-site between July 5th of 1995 and July 27th of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you please put your initials in the bottom right-hand corner and then today's date, 11 January 2012.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And can I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just to summarise and round that off, it's your conclusion that the bodies from that grave were placed there in a single interment between the dates of 5 and 27 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the last area I want to ask you a couple of questions about are the probable blindfolds that were recovered from Lazete 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if we can go back to 65 ter 2482; that's P4135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Page 23 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's page 22 of the physical report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's sufficient to upload the English version only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page. Is it correct -- right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No. It's the page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's the next page. You said hard copy page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You're right. That's the correct page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: At the top of this page you describe how on 89 bodies there was strips of material tied around the head and placed over the face or directly associated to the head. And you concluded that these were probably used as blindfolds. Now, can you explain why you concluded that these 89 strips of pink material were probably blindfolds and not something else. For example, some kind of ceremonial headband.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In -- what we were encountering here was a mass grave with no clear funerary practices, disorganised bodies, no respect was shown as far as the way the bodies were buried. It seemed to be that this is concurrent with a site of deposition of or execution of bodies, and the pieces of cloth which were very similar seemed to have uniformity. And in most of the cases seemed to be covering the eyes. The term "probable" was used because in some instances they were not covering the eyes and they were covering the mouth or in a couple of instances they might have moved up to the forehead. But in general they were covering the eyes. And also because we found another 37 strips of material very particular, again scalloped edges and pink. And we believe that these could also have been used as blindfolds and might have fell off the bodies. I think you can see some of those -- there's an image of those in the report as well. The colour I think is also something very important. Pink is not some -- is not a colour that you would use to wear as a headband in a combat situation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You found 34 strips of the same type of material in the Lazete 2C grave over the other side of the railway tracks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Let me check on the number, but I believe so. Yes, 34 strips of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peccerelli. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, I'm afraid the markings by this witness of Lazete 1 and Lazete 2 on aerial image have been lost. Do you think we need to do that exercise again or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I could take him very briefly to the photo and just have him quickly mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Could we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It was 65 ter 3199 and page 146 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And when this comes up, Mr. Peccerelli, if you can just mark for us the Lazete 1 and Lazete 2 sites.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you could circle the actual grave areas within --

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And then initialise and date.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Peccerelli. First of all, I'd like to thank you for meeting up with the Defence. I hope that that will help us conduct this examination as simply as possible. I see that Mr. Mitchell even used that interview of ours to clarify a few matters, so even he had some benefit from it and I thank him for it. I would like to start with the very last matter. On page 22, in response to Mr. Mitchell's question about the possible bands, or rather, you say these are possible blindfolds, he asked whether this was a ceremonial thing. You brought that into question -- actually, the argumentation you provided was that the burial was not dignified and was not carried out in accordance with religious customs and rites. Was it your understanding that these bands are used during religious burial ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, no, they are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that was your answer. In a way you expressed your doubt, you doubted that these were ceremonial bands because there were no other elements that would be involved in a dignified religious burial. Do you know - and up until our interview you had not known about this, your hosts in Bosnia had not informed you about this - do you know of the custom of wearing these headbands during combat and they're worn on the forehead. And then if tissue decays, then the headband may fall down or slide down. Do you know that this was customary among the Islamic fighters?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you bring up the page of his report which shows the probable blindfold. E-court page is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: E-court page is 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 23. Thank you, Mr. Mitchell. Mr. Karadzic, were you referring to these pictures when you asked the witness about the ceremonial or customary thing? Or your question was in general?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood things correctly, Mr. Mitchell brought this into doubt -- or rather, offered the possibility of doubting whether these were ceremonial headbands. On page 22, Mr. Peccerelli said that he had not seen any other signs of a ceremonial burial, and that therefore the conclusion could be drawn that perhaps these were not headbands but rather blindfolds. This led me to think that Mr. Peccerelli perhaps thought that bands were used during burials, not during fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what was your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that the case and does Mr. Peccerelli know that these bands were not used during burials? On the contrary, they were used during fighting, combat. So the absence of other elements of a religious burial does not say a thing about these bands because these bands are not used during burial ceremonies, but rather during a person's life and when that person goes into combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we heard the answer from the witness. Let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So nevertheless, out of an abundance of caution, you used the word "probable." What led you to this relativisation, or rather, this reservation? What led you to do that? For example, these very same victims, did they have their hands tied or did they only have these blindfolds or bands on their heads?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: What led me and the team to put "probable" was because some of them were not placed directly over the eyes and had been moved due to the movement of the bodies being placed in the grave as well as decomposition. Also the fact that we also found 37 more. They were not directly on the bodies but because they were the same type of material, mostly all of the same colour, and mostly all with scalloped edges, we believed that this could also have been probable blindfolds and that's what led us to use that term. As far as -- let's see, two of them had their hands tied behind their back and those are listed in the report. The rest we found no evidence of them having restraints. Only, like I mentioned at the beginning, there was a third body that had a strip of material that was placed around both thighs and then went into the lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that under such circumstances when people cannot be differentiated on the basis of race, language, faith, combatants are marked by such ribbons or other markings in order to prevent friendly fire?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that these two persons, these two victims, with tied hands did not have any blindfolds on?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: You would have to give me a second to check. These are body 549 and 560 according to the report. Yes, body 549 did not have a blindfold and body 560 -- however, body 560 did according to the exhumation form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where was that band in the case of that particular body?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Over the eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any explanation or any way of understanding why people who were being shot at and who did not have their hands tied would suffer having some blindfold on their eyes when, quite simply, they could tear them off by moving their hands?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: My only explanation for that would be the overwhelming amount of ballistic evidence at the site, and to think that they were probably -- probably shot rather quickly and did not have a chance or were probably afraid to take them off if they were told not to take them off. If they would, they would probably be shot. That's my only explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how and in which way did you rule out the possibility that these were not executions in the case of persons who did not have their hands tied? How did you rule out that possibility? Actually, during our interview you said that no one had informed you about 44 months of heavy fighting in that area, 44 months of heavy fighting. No one told you that you might come across such graves and such victims. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, nobody informed me that there was 44 months of fighting in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was it beyond reasonable doubt and by applying which method did you rule out the possibility that these victims were the victims of combat? Basically you were seriously restricted by this lack of information to the effect that there had been 44 months of heavy fighting. Had you known about that, you probably would have done things differently or at least some things. Could you rule out the possibility of these people having died in combat?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, here I must say that to answer this question you cannot only do it with the excavation part of the investigation. This type of an investigation has to be approached with a multi-disciplinary approach and I would need the information, first of all, of the traumas that each one of these bodies was sustained. There is specific information, there's actual studies conducted by Dr. Snow and Jose Pablo Baraybar that shows that during 60 years and 25 different conventional combat you only expect to have fatal wounds in 0.199 of the wounds of the people wounded which means that only two out of ten wounds are fatal in combat. And this is shown in 25 different combats all over the world during 60 years. If I had the information of the traumas that these people suffered, I could probably put them into this frequency of fatal wound formula and tell you that with a high degree of probability. The other thing I would do is I know for a fact that ICMP has been working on the DNA identification of these bodies. I would see if these are, in fact, the victims of Srebrenica that have been identified here and that would also help me to ascertain whether the testimony that says that the people were taken to this site and executed here are the same people that were, in fact, taken from Srebrenica. So I would definitely answer your question more completely with all of that information, but the excavation part of this investigation tells us that we did find a -- once again, a primary grave with 127 bodies. Two other bodies were found in a drainage ditch. Two of these bodies had hands tied behind their back and 89 bodies had these cloths over their faces. The way the bodies were placed in the grave were -- gives me at least -- leads me to believe that they were pushed in with some type of machinery, and that also put some of the top-soil within the bodies. And also the fact that I -- we did not find any markings on these headbands, we did not find any weapons, I mean all of those things would have to be taken into account for me to be able to make that type of a conclusion. The evidence here tells me that there's nothing that I can see that leads me to believe that this was combat deaths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are conducting your cross-examination not only in the capacity of an accused but also as counsel who represent yourself. So I'm asking you in that latter capacity, is it your case that the people whose pictures we are seeing in front of us died as a result of combat?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, my case is that an enormous number of victims died in combat. Yesterday we heard from a witness that we -- that they left behind the victims of bombings and the Serbs later buried them. That is what we were told by a witness, a Muslim, who was part of that column that was leaving. I can prove that the presence of leafs and a surface layer clearly indicates that bodies were gathered from the surface and then interred in a newly dug grave. Even Mr. Peccerelli himself says that there was some dust there, that is to say, soil coming from the surface. That means that these bodies had spent a certain amount of time on the surface.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that theory applies to both Lazete 1 and Lazete 2? Is that your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I don't know whether there were some executions, but blindfolds without having these persons' hands tied are illogical. We saw video clips of Islamic fighters with the headbands going into combat. Mr. Peccerelli himself says that sometimes these bands were on the eyes or on the nose or further down, so I am challenging executions in obvious cases. Let the Prosecution prove, for instance, who executed 12 tied men. That is not debatable at all. However, there were so many victims of 44 months of heavy fighting, warfare, and all of that is being put under "executions" and that is what I am challenging and that is what I can prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, is that the only explanation of the varying degree of degradation of the bodies involved? How and in which way do you rule out the possibility of burials taking place in several stages, that is to say, after fighting existing graves were increased by adding further bodies into them. Isn't that another viable possibility?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In Lazete 1 and Lazete 2, that is not a possibility. These graves were homogenous in their shape, their depth. The bodies were placed with no strata of foreign soil between them. All they had was clumps of top-soil that were, again, a result of the bodies being pushed in with machinery at one single time. During my experience, once again, of excavating over 1400 different cases and close to 20.000 sets of human remains, we can tell as anthropologists and archaeologists when graves are disturbed. And, as a matter of fact, it is customary in Guatemala when a cemetery runs out of room to bury several bodies in one grave. And even the people who work at the cemeteries disturb the other bodies when they do this. So you expect to see some degree of disturbance in the graves, definitely different degree of preservation as far as the anatomical positioning of the bones in relationship to each other, in other words, the articulation of the bones and of the bodies. There's nothing in these two graves that tell us that. There's no evidence of these graves coming at a later time or on top of earlier graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you speaking about the procedure of burial in Guatemala in war time or peace time?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I would have to say both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am a little bit baffled now by something. You said that you believe or that you established - and if you did, would you please tell us how - that before the 5th of July there were no burials in these two locations. Is that correct? Were you able to rule that out?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: What I said was that I believe that this -- these two graves were dug between the date of July 5th and July 27th, and that was established because of the aerial images we have. The fact that there were no previous burials was established by the stratographic methodology used to conduct the archeological excavation and exhumation of the bodies. In other words, like I mentioned previously, the uniformity of the graves, the way the bodies were laid on top of each other, the articulation of these bodies, it's a clear sign that these graves did not disturb other graves. We also don't have remains from other bodies from previous excavations being disturbed by these bodies. There are no features within any one of these two graves that these interrupted previous burials. What we do have in both graves is that when these were dug there was a pre-existing excavation that carried within it a water-pipe and we found that. We were able to see that these two graves cut into pre-existing ditches that carried water-pipes in them. So this type of evidence is something that we can see in the ground. We did not see this with any other type of grave. We did not see any feature whatsoever that would lead us to believe that there was previous graves in any one of the two locations where we exhumed Lazete 1 and Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These two bodies in Lazete 1 that were found in the canal, was the canal filled up?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: If you're referring to the drainage ditch, yes, it had soil over them. These were not graves but the bodies were on the surface but covered with soil. And these bodies also had the probable blindfolds and they were in the same stage of decomposition as the ones in the graves. As I said in my report, I believe that these two bodies were -- probably fell there during the robbing incident that occurred later during that year and were covered over by the machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, to what extent did these ditches correspond to the direction of the water-pipes or did they intersect each other? More precisely, at what angle did the damage to the water-pipes occur or did the direction of the ditch or the canal and the water-pipes correspond exactly in direction and degree?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: There is an image --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we upload it? I think it's e-court page 18 if I'm correct in number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the report it's page number 12 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That will be e-court page 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you can see evidence of this pre-existing excavation of the water-pipe, and in the image below, the -- a little higher, please, it says figure 19, in that one you can see how the grave was dug on top of this and intersects the water-pipe. Now, if you go to the lower image, I would say that the -- the question was what angle. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The bottom part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bottom part, there we go. It looks like the grave sort of falls obliquely over -- over the ditch that carried the water-pipe -- not the ditch, the excavation that carried this water-pipe. The drainage ditch ran in the southern part of the grave, more or less where the arrows are coming from. So we're talking about different features. We're talking about a drainage ditch that was sort of a natural feature in the soil and then we're talking about an excavation that carried a water-pipe in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say with respect to page 18, hard copy page 17? We upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This what you can see here in the background, this is a secondary pipe that just fell along the ditch. We did not -- it's not mapped in because it wasn't -- there wasn't an excavation that the grave itself cut into. The other one we found particularly interesting because the grave itself intersected that excavation and led us to see that there was a pre-existing water-pipe that had been severed and later reconnected. Once again, these two bodies were not in the grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these the two bodies that were found in the canal or the channel, the one that you referred to as the drainage ditch?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Peccerelli, how did you rule out the possibility that this was an old trench from which there was firing, a firing position which after it was captured was widened and used as a location for burial?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say that that was not something that we considered. What I did -- I mean, what you can see here, there is a grave, a mass grave, 10, 15 metres away. And if you look at -- there's an image, one of the aerial images on report page 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 12 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could -- yeah, the lower -- there we go, that one. The location of those two bodies is directly where those -- there's a -- I don't know if you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could mark it. See, these images are from September, September 7th and September 27th, and you can see how the grave was one size on September 7th and then there was a disturbance again where you can see -- you can actually see tracks, you can see tracks here and you can also see tracks here. Those two bodies laid around this area here. So the conclusion that these two bodies were a result of the robbing excavation comes from the evidence seen in the aerial images.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you rule out the possibility that the grave was refilled, that there were subsequent burials there? How did you conclude that the changes were a result of additional burial because fighting was still underway?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Once again, the grave showed no evidence of having any bodies, any additional bodies, being put into it. What it had was evidence of bodies being taken out of it. And this was shown by the creation of body parts around the robbing excavations as well as the truncation or segmentation of bodies around the edges of the robbing excavation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you kindly initial and date this marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it working?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. We'll admit this marked photo as Exhibit -- as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1989, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, would similar things happen with bodies that would have been collected from the surface using machinery from a different location which had spent a longer period of time on the surface which were degraded, segmented, would those bodies be damaged if they were brought to this location? Would we have fragmented bodies?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if you had a surface -- bodies that laid on the surface for prolonged periods of time would show evidence of -- decomposition works very differently when bodies are left in the surface. You would have probably quicker skeletonisation. You would probably have gnaw marks from animals, sun exposure to the bones which causes bleaching, probably disarticulation due to also animal activity. If you then recovered those bodies and placed them within this grave, they would look very differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I direct your attention to paragraph 8 -- to section VIII of Lazete 2 and to its characteristics. And you state here that the grave represents the place of multiple mass primary burial of human remains covered by dug-over earth and with yellow --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We need time to find the place where Mr. Karadzic is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, interpreters have difficulty following you. Why don't we upload it. The second report, page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please see where it says below the bodies -- and immediately below the same bodies clumps of earth were found surface layer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to Lazete 1 or 2?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking about what we're seeing on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid this is related to Lazete 1. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think Dr. Karadzic is reading from Lazete 2. It's 65 ter 11151 and page 14 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's section VIII, the grave and its properties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but the title of both documents on the same page was identical. That's the reason of confusion. Thank you. Is this it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that it is and I think that it's instructive and we should keep it on the screen for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you agree that it states here that below the -- "large pieces of turf, top-soil, and clay were found under and directly over the bodies within the grave. The mixed nature of the soil grave fill and the disorganised interment of the bodies was probably the result of the bodies being pushed into the grave ..." and so on. How does the thesis seem to you, Mr. Peccerelli, that the bodies were gathered up from a surface whereby the machinery also caught up pieces of turf that happened to be below and above the bodies? Are you able to rule this out?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, I think we are saying exactly the same thing. I'm saying that these bodies were on the surface and were pushed into the grave, and that that took some of the -- you see -- on this picture you can see how there is a mound of dirt in the background. When you dig a grave you have to displace the -- to make the hole you have to take the dirt out of it. So there's a combination. Let's say the bodies were laying left of this grave and then they were pushed in, you were -- you're going to take some of the top-soil and some of the soil that was excavated along with the bodies if you use machinery. It's different than when you use -- when you place them in the grave manually when you would only pick up the bodies and place them usually in order and usually with no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Why don't we lower the picture to see the entire picture. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Peccerelli.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I think I'm done. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How can we rule out and can we rule out a loader gathering the bodies from the surface, whereby also it would catch turf below and above the bodies. So it would not be bodies pushed in but being gathered from different locations and transported together? How can you rule that out? Because pushing does not necessarily mean that turf would be disturbed that is below the bodies. A loader with a very sharp bucket definitely would collect or pick up turf.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I -- what you're describing specifically is exactly what I'm saying. Obviously I cannot rule it out. That is the same exact mechanism whether it be a bulldozer or a front-loader. Both machines have the capacity to turn over top-soil and pick it up and then are delicate enough to only pick up the bodies. So that can happen. Obviously the evidence here not only within the grave but around the grave suggests that there was shooting going on in this specific place and, you know, because of its isolated location it would be logical to think that the bodies in the grave came from the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But also there is the possibility that they came from a different one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I guess the possibility does exist, however remote it might seem contemplating the whole investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what does it mean that a place is a multiple mass primary interment site of human remains?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, once again, this is a -- what that means by definition is a grave. Primary which means that it was -- for the first time that location was being used to deposit bodies into it. Multiple bodies means that there were more than one. There is no specific number. In this case you would have to look at how many bodies the PHR exhumations collected. We only collected 16 bodies and I believe 26 body parts from this exhumation, but that's -- that's what it means, that there was -- this was a hole that was created and turned into a grave when multiple bodies were placed into it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at that part of the text in English on the screen so that we can see how this "multiple" looks in English. Can we look at the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Peccerelli, what did you follow when you were excavating? What did you follow -- [In English] Just a moment. "The grave is a multiple mass primary interment site of human remains ..." "Multiple." [Interpretation] Does that not mean that the burial was carried out in several goes?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I can see how there is a misunderstanding but that's not what I meant. What I meant was that this was a primary mass grave, and in this specific case you have to remember that there was four different excavations on this site. The original or primary excavation of the site; the later robbing excavation of the site; the later PHR excavations, which were two; and then finally the excavation we carried out in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it's still not clear to me why you use the term "multiple" instead of mass grave.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: "Multiple" meaning more than one body, same thing as "mass." I did not mean several different interments. That would not be -- see, the terms are contradictory. You cannot have in a primary grave multiple because the repeating excavation into a primary grave would make a secondary interment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how would you describe or call a grave where for the first time in several stages a number of bodies are buried and bodies are added? How would you refer to that type of grave?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Well, the original grave would be a primary grave with secondary interment into it, and each one of those secondary interments would be described as a secondary excavation and a secondary deposit of human remains into it. They would be considered disturbances of the primary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Even though these additional bodies would be buried for the first and only time, you would still refer to it as a secondary grave even though those bodies that were additionally buried would actually be buried for the first and only time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The term "primary" refers to the incursion into the soil, not the body itself. So you're talking about the excavation being the primary excavation. Any excavation you conduct into an existing grave would be a secondary one and the patterns of it are very different. So you can deposit a body for the first time, but if you open an existing primary grave you will be conducting a secondary interment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, I'm a doctor, and from what I know, secondary burial means that one body was buried in one place and then reburied. How is this possible that your terminology is different from mine? A secondary grave means that the body was transferred from another place and buried for the second time. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: You see, we are talking about different things. You're talking about bodies being removed and then reburied in a different place. I'm talking about incursions into a primary grave which is something that we don't see here so you're talking about something that did not occur. We don't have any secondary disturbances of the primary excavation here. What we have is a single event with posterior disturbances of the grave to extract bodies not to put bodies in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you explain the surface layer between certain bodies? There would be a layer of bodies, then there would be a layer of surface or top-soil, then a thin layer of top-soil, then another layer of bodies. If not by additional burial, how do you explain that this top-soil layer was over one set of bodies and below another set of bodies?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Once again, they are not layers, they are pieces. They are pieces of turf, top-soil. These are not stratography layers that cover an entire area. These are just pieces of turf and top-soil and clay. Again, I explain it by the same definition you gave, machinery picking up bodies and taking top-soil and pieces of clay with it and then throwing them into the grave, pushing them into the grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time -- about time to take a break now, and given that we have a somewhat longer break due to technical difficulties and that we have about three hours from now on until the end of today, so we are minded to have two short breaks, i.e., two half-an-hour breaks and with two one-hour sessions. I hope that would be okay with the staff. Okay. We'll do that. We'll take a half-an-hour break now and resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peccerelli, when did you carry out this exhumation?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: We began on the 13th of July, 2000, all the way to the 8th of August of the same year. Yeah, between the 13th of July to the 8th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was the man in charge during that exhumation? Who was the main person there, if you will?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: You mean from ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The team leader at the time was Brian Strongman. He is, I think, a retired Canadian Mounted Police if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 you say that a senior forensic archaeologist appointed a supervisor. Who were the two in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: In this particular case, since I was the deputy in an absence of Richard Wright who was contracted as the senior forensic archaeologist for the entire season, I was the acting senior forensic archaeologist and I assigned different archaeologists to be the co-ordinator at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who did you appoint as the supervisor?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: The senior archaeologists all got a chance to be supervisors. So, for example, Ian Hanson, Claudia Rivera, Jon Sterenberg, Gaille McKinnon as well. There is a list of the people who participated in the team, and we had senior personnel and junior personnel. The four people that I mentioned, Claudia Rivera, Gaille McKinnon, Ian Hanson and Jon Sterenberg, were the co-ordinators or the supervisors at the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please cast a glance at chapter V, where you say in paragraph 4 that the senior forensic archaeologist shall appoint an exhumation supervisor, shall direct the excavators within the grave. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Once again, one week it was Claudia Rivera, another week it was Jon Sterenberg, Gaille McKinnon and Ian Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Are you the first and only ones who dealt with Lazete 2?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No and no. We were not the first and we were not the only ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who, when, and to what extent worked before you at that location?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: From limited knowledge I have, it was a team of Physicians for Human Rights led by Dr. Bill Haglund sometime in 1996. To what extent, I believe they only worked in two areas of grave -- of Lazete 2. They found two body concentrations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. And then after that, four years after that, you worked there; right?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct, four years after that I worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you describe that in your report, namely, that you came after this intervention, or rather, after this work of Doctors for Human Rights, Dr. Haglund, Dr. Kirschner and so on?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I believe so. I would have to find it, if you give me a second. That would be on page 2 of the Lazete report, in the summary findings, section (f). "In 1996, the PHR exhumation team conducted an investigation at this very site. They identified two graves, they named these Lazete 2A and Lazete 2 B."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what happened then? Do you know that under the supervision of Dr. Kirschner an exhumation was carried out and conclusions were drawn up in relation to the cause and mode of death as well as a revision of the final autopsy findings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can just clarify the question. I think the evidence is Dr. Haglund was in charge of the exhumation. Dr. Kirschner was the chief pathologist at the morgue. So if that could just be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you content with that clarification, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can understand that from the documents that I see before me and that I'm going to tender when Dr. Haglund comes. However, this is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at that point in time exhumations were carried out and that autopsies were carried out and that autopsy reports were drawn up that were revised with the assistance of Mr. McCloskey, the legal advisor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I had knowledge of the exhumations and I guess it's logical for them to have rendered reports, but that's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How does that affect your work?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Lazete 2, is that the same location or not?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No -- yes, of course it is. If you mean -- I mean how does the report affect my work or how does the excavation affect my work?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does their excavation affect your conclusions on layers, positions, and so on?
