So somebody touched the grave four years before you did, under conditions of heavy rainfall, bad weather in general, and so on, and then after that, you draw conclusions about the content of the soil there and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Actually, as I mentioned earlier, this grave, it was 37.7 metres in length. When the PHR team exhumed, they did not -- as I understand it, they did not conduct a surface recovery or a removal of the top-soil or the layer on top of the grave. What they did was -- I believe was trench and when they did that they found two accumulations of bodies and they named these Lazete 2A and B. The way we dealt with that was we had the initial excavation of the grave. Then you have the robbing excavations. Then you have the PHR excavations. And then you have our excavations. And these are clearly marked in the report. And simply what we did was describe what we found. What they had done was similar to the robbing excavations except they were more thorough because they removed the bodies by hand, they exhumed these bodies by hand, whereas during the subsequent robbing excavations they were removed by machinery and created body parts and also segmented some of the bodies that were left. If you allow me, I'll show you what page is this on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about page 16, e-court 17?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- yes. It will be coming up. If necessary, you can mark the drawings here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The initial grave was the entire extent. This is what we call Lazete 2C, which is [marks]. Then you have robbing excavations A, which occurred here, and B which occurred here. The PHR team located --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we change the colour now to blue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. They excavated this area here and this area here, from which I believe or at least I was told there they recovered complete bodies. So what you have here is similar to what you had in Lazete 1, that there was removal of bodies and segmentation in the two areas marked in red, but the two areas marked in green, the bodies were not removed and they were found complete. Those are the two areas that the Physicians for Human Rights team exhumed in 1996, and we later took out -- again using the stratographic method took out the contents of the grave and left the profile of the grave. That's how we can find those features. Shall I ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if you want, I can also do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if I understand this correctly, there were two exhumations in this grave before you came there. However, did they cover up the grave after that or did they just leave it open?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: When we found it, the grave was covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, that marked diagram will be admitted as D1990.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So before you there were at least two excavations and possibly some unauthorised excavation. Does that mean that you came to a grave where there had been different physical manipulations and that then you drew your own conclusions?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there had been an investigation about that first one. C.E. Moore, have you heard of that person who worked with Dr. Kirschner and Dr. Haglund? I don't know if it's a lady or a gentleman, but this person did take part in this excavation in 1996.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wasn't there in 1996. I don't know who you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of professional challenges, disputes, conflicts in relation to Lazete 2 and that there had been some investigation that had been carried out among an association of pathologists or something like that in America?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No. The only thing I heard prior to the excavation in Lazete 2 during the excavation of Lazete 1 was that someone from the original team said that there was still bodies in that grave and that they wanted it to be exhumed. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Doctor, now you mentioned, Doctor, that you drew your conclusions when you came to the grave where there had been different physical manipulations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, would this have affected your conclusion in any way at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what we can see was that there had been interventions into the grave and that was documented. But, you know, in the end what we concluded that this grave had been disturbed several times and we concluded more on our findings and less on what was not there. So, in other words, the original contents of this grave I -- I cannot testify to. I don't know how many bodies were exhumed by the Physicians for Human Rights team nor do I know how many bodies were taken away from those two robbing areas. But from the size of this grave, it is a substantial-sized grave, there was probably a lot of bodies in there. Would it have affected -- I mean, obviously if I would have excavated this grave before any of this had happened, the results would have been different because the findings would have been different. I don't know if that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that during that first excavation when the conclusions were being formulated, Mr. Peter McCloskey, who represented the OTP, took part in that drafting process?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, I don't know that -- I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you hear of this investigation carried out in San Antonio in relation to the first exhumation of 1996?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't heard of any such investigation --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Inquiry, sort of inquiry and -- [Interpretation] You haven't heard of that; right?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: No, personally, no. I don't know what it pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This first exhumation from 1996 was professionally contested and led to professional disputes within the ranks of that team from 1996, and all of this led to an inquiry in San Antonio and a professional debate as well. I'm not aware of the ultimate conclusions reached, but I certainly know that this had been investigated. Now, was it a court of honour or something like that, but anyway, there was this debate in San Antonio and there was a professional dispute with regard to that team.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you asked me to explain what this was all about. So it means that that first team worked and then that led to a dispute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness said he didn't know. Let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But my understanding was that the witness wanted me to clarify what it was that I meant. [In English] "I don't know what pertains to." [Interpretation] Line 4, page 50, and that led me to try to explain. Could we have the previous page now, the one with the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was it that you followed in the case of this grave? What was it that you followed in order to get to this shape?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous page. Can somebody please help me with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 16, Lazete 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This one is different from the one we had had in colour. Tell me, what was it that you followed? I mean, how did you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Okay. As I mentioned earlier, what we do is a stratographic excavation. In other words, we excavate -- we remove the contents of the grave strata by strata from the inside and we do this by separating the fill from the original soil. Now, what you see here on the walls is the original -- some of it is the original grave, others is parts that have been altered by robbing excavations. And you can see this on the left side where there's actual pieces that were taken away. If you want I can mark more or less where by -- you can see within those are machine marks made as they were taking parts of the grave away. And the parts that are higher, where the bodies are, are the ones that were left behind. This is the same methodology we used in Lazete 1. And the difference is that the fill is loose, so it's fairly easy to remove.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I meant was actually how you got the idea to move in this direction and how to dig such a deep trench, if you will. Were you guided by the previous excavation of 1996 or something else in that effort?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you mentioned that the previous team in 1996 had found some bodies in a trench. How was it that you ruled out the possibility of that having been a combat position during one of those 44 months and that it was then used for a burial?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Once again, I didn't know about the 44 months you mentioned, so it wasn't something I had to rule out. utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: What about this, where is the water-pipe that you referred to? Was it in this grave?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is this diagonal line that we see, but I don't see the marking that lies north to east? What does that line indicate?

utterances.text: Change the colour, yes. Let us change the colour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that's the one you mean, that's the reconnection of the water-pipe. Once it was severed by the grave, it had to be reconnected up top. So it's another water-pipe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's not legible very much. It says "new pipe." Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then the -- on the old pipe you wrote down "pipe out" in both places? The characters are so small. It reads --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says "new pipe" and "pipe" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And "pipe disconnected," how does it read? With an arrow -- left to the arrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Pipes reconnected." Thank you.

utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI
utterances.text: Oh, they marked two trenches which they did directly over the grave. You can't see them, let's see, because they were extracted as they removed the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then can we please save this if it cannot be marked. I would like to draw your attention now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So did you refer to Lazete 2A and B?

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI

utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the victims had a certain number of wrist-watches, pocket-watches, documents, and some personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.text: Thank you. You were not permanently employed at the OTP, while the investigators were; is that correct?

utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did any members of the Defence have access to you to tell you whatever it is that they had to tell you or was it just the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI

utterances.speaker: FREDY PECCERELLI

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Mr. President, I would just like to answer a question that the Trial Chamber posed to me last time I was here. utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. In March 1995, Colonel Joseph Kingori, a United Nations Military Observer, was stationed in Srebrenica. At the time he held the rank of major. The Colonel's main duty was to monitor and report any violations to the cease-fire agreement. He had contact with all parties, conveying messages from one side to the other and attempting to bridge their differences. Major Nikolic and Colonel Vukovic were the -- were Colonel Kingori's main contact within the VRS. Colonel Kingori described the lack of food in Srebrenica. Water and electricity were also scarce. Some of this was due to the VRS's restrictions on aid convoys coming into the enclave. Leading up to July 1995, the VRS pushed further and further into the enclave itself. The colonel occasionally attempted to penetrate behind VRS lines to observe the military situation. There were times he could not reach even the enclave's internal borders because the VRS stood in the way. During this time he was only armed with a pencil and a notebook. The colonel was one of two UN military observers present in Srebrenica during the fall of the enclave. On the morning of July 6 he was awoken by heavy shelling that continued on the 7th, 8th, and 9th. At first the shelling seemed directed outside the town, as though to push the population of the enclave into the town itself. Then the shelling changed, targeting the town as though to drive the population out entirely and towards the DutchBat compound at Potocari. During the shelling, the two military observers were alternately inside the bunker of the PTT building filing reports and going out on patrol to examine the damage done by the shelling. Even from inside the bunker, the military observers could hear and count the shells. Outside the bunker they could see the shells falling. The colonel observed that, among other weaponry, the VRS was using tanks to fire missiles. This was in contrast to any weaponry the ABiH had inside the enclave. The colonel testified that even if there were a few guns held within the enclave, they were old weapons unable to withstand or provoke the kind of fire-power levelled by the VRS. On July 9th, the military observers left Srebrenica for Potocari. The enclave had already been encircled by the VRS. The colonel testified that it was as though the Muslims were being crushed in one place. The population was forced to look for an exit, and like the military observers, they streamed to Potocari in the thousands to seek refuge with the UN. It was not an organised exodus. On July 10th, the shelling continued. The Colonel could hear it very well himself from the DutchBat compound. The military observers also had a set of eyes still within the town of Srebrenica. An UNMO translator went back to Srebrenica from Potocari, so as to report on shells landing within the town. He had been with the UN for two years and could competently report on artillery. The Colonel attended a meeting with DutchBat and representatives of the ABiH. The purpose was to discuss an ultimatum issued from the VRS that Muslims needed to leave the enclave. By the end of the day on July 11th, the Potocari compound was filled with Muslim civilians, both inside the parameters of the compound and outside the fence. On July 12th, VRS soldiers arrived at the DutchBat compound. Those soldiers took up positions all around it, observing the whole area and the approximately 30.000 refugees gathered there. The Colonel went out of the compound to investigate. He saw General Mladic in a field by the compound and then the two at first discussed informalities and then the events. Mladic told Kingori that the VRS would provide buses for the evacuation of the refugees. Within 20 or 30 minutes of this conversation, buses began arriving. VRS soldiers herded women and children onto the buses, but Kingori saw them pull aside men and boys who were 14, 15, and 16. The men and boys were sent to the white house. The separation of them from the women was traumatic. There were senior VRS officers present as crying families were pushed apart. Kingori approached Mladic again, complaining that the white house was overcrowded. Mladic replied that as far as he was concerned, the people were comfortable. He took Kingori to the white house, where Kingori saw men seated on top of one another and with no space between them. Mladic refused to allow the Colonel to enter the house. Men were taken from the white house and put on separate buses from the women and children. Young boys were shoved onto the buses as well and the Colonel tried to ask their ages. If a boy answered "14," the Colonel took him back to the VRS soldiers and away from the buses. The Colonel would then turn and see more buses -- excuse me, more boys pushed onto the buses by the VRS. The men were also forced on the buses without their belongings. They left behind everything they had, including their identification cards. According to the Colonel, this was an indicator that something bad was going to happen. He explained it meant that these people, whatever was going to be done to them, it would be very difficult to identify them later. The Colonel tried to make a record of the men's identities. He asked the men to shout their names to him so that he could make some record of them. He testified that this is one of the saddest moments he witnessed in Srebrenica. On July 13th, the Colonel tried to investigate rumours that Muslim civilians were being taken behind a building by VRS soldiers. He was prevented by the VRS from going to the location but heard a gun-shot from the building. On the 13th as well, the Colonel went with representatives of MSF to evacuate patients from Srebrenica hospital to the compound. Some didn't want to leave, but the Colonel was told by VRS soldiers at the hospital that if he did not take the patients with him, they would be killed. The removal of refugees from the compound by the VRS continued, and by the 14th, the refugees were gone and only the wounded remained. Military observers helped MSF prepare a list of wounded and of local staff to try to safely evacuate them. This was negotiated with the VRS including Major Nikolic and the VRS civilian affairs officer Miroslav Deronjic. During the negotiations, Professor Koljevic was also called. On the 18th of July, the wounded were evacuated by the ICRC and a few days later the Colonel left Srebrenica along with MSF, DutchBat, and the local staff. Mr. President, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, when did you retire from the Kenyan Air Force?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I retired in August 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And after that, for what organisation did you work?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, after retiring from the Kenya Air Force I joined the National Disaster Operations Centre as the deputy director.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you explain to us what your role was there, what your job was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the role -- our roles at the National Disaster Operations Centre was to monitor and co-ordinate disaster management, that includes training and response and also risk reduction in the whole country.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, when did you finish your contract there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, my contract was for four years, which ended last year in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what do you do now?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Right now, Your Honour, I'm working together with the Moi University, that is the local university, in training of disaster -- district disaster management committees on disaster management in their local areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, we understand that from March 1995 until July 1995 you were a United Nations Military Observer in Srebrenica. Can you tell us generally the duties of a military observer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the duties of a military observer are diverse, but most of the apparent ones that we had was the monitoring of the violation to the cease-fire agreement that was already in place and also ensuring that those who were coming in to bring in aid, that is, in terms of food, water, through UN agencies like UNHCR, were getting a clearance to get into the enclave and also were assisted in getting out of the enclave safely. That is just a few among many others that we had. Also I think it's important to bring one more, that is bringing the warring factions together through holding of meetings together in with different functions. And then whatever we are told from this side we inform the other side so that we can bridge the gap between the two and so that we could be able to bring them together.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 5 of your statement, it's noted that military observers were never armed. Can you tell us why this is so?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms it is difficult to explain, but normally a military observer in any UN mission is never armed. The reason being if you're not armed, you are able to go to any area without fear that somebody might harm you because of the weapon you have or the other person fearing that you might harm them in case you have a weapon. So you have a free way of going to either side of the warring factions without fear at all. That is the main reason. But also it's good to note that we used to have a book and a pen on which to write notes that we could see on the ground or hear or even investigate which through both their functions it was a very strong weapon in that whatever we wrote was taken very seriously by the UN system.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, in order to become a military observer, what minimal level of experience must a candidate have?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, first and foremost, to be a military observer you must be a senior military officer. Here we are talking about from the rank of major and above, and you had to have -- for you to have reached that rank you definitely must have served for ten years in the military. So for sure you had to be a senior and experienced officer because whatever judgement that you were going to make in the field could have a lot of repercussions and also you are expected to make judgements according to your experience and knowledge that you already have.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 19423, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, after you left Srebrenica, were you and the other two military observers debriefed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we were debriefed in UNMO headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the other two observers who were with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: The other two observers, Your Honour, were Major David Tetteh from Ghana and Major Andre de Haan from Holland.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, we see the document in front of us and if we look at paragraph 2, it notes that there were three of you and it also says that the Kenyan officer took the lead role in the debriefing. Is that referring to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now if we can go to the next page, please, and we're going to go to paragraph 4 and this is a paragraph that talks about the VRS take-over of OP Echo. And just for the record, Colonel Kingori, in front of you is also a copy of this document if that makes it any easier for you. Actually physically, it's one of those pieces of paper. Paragraph 4 refers to OP Echo but it notes that OP Echo took place on the 3rd of July. Is that the correct date of the overthrow of OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was on the 3rd but not of July. I remember very well and it is in my notes that it was in June, that is, the previous month.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the significance of the road upon which OP Echo was located?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was a very important road that led to the southern side of the enclave through an area we used to call Zeleni Jadar and which had some mineral deposits, that is, bauxite, and also there were some factories in that area including a timber factory, and it was one of the vantage points that any military would have wanted to occupy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, as a result of the BSA successful attack on OP Echo, what was the response by DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, DutchBat tried to hold that place but they could not be able to hold so they moved backwards a bit because the BSA could have attacked them at any time, so they moved behind and left the OP.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm now going to move to paragraph 9, which is the following page, and this talks about OP Foxtrot and firing on the town of Srebrenica. Were you in Srebrenica on July 9th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was in Srebrenica on July 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, in fact, we're going to talk about the days before when you were there as well. You describe extensively the shelling in your statement. But in this debriefing you also described the inhabitants of Srebrenica being paralysed and confused. Can you tell us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This was due to the shelling that was going on, in that the BSA were shelling both outside the town and later on inside the town, so it caused a lot of confusion which actually could have been the main aim of the shelling, to make sure that everybody is confused. So they did not know what to do or where to go and there was a lot of confusion. We could see it inside the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as a result of that confusion, did you see people running all over the place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was the most evident thing, in that people were running all over, they didn't know where to go, where to hide, what to do. And so we could see it and then there was a lot of fear in their eyes and everything, but of course it was caused by the shelling that was still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at paragraph 11, a little bit further down, you noted that: "The BSA knew of this weakness in the chain of command and timed their attack to exploit it." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this weakness in the chain of command was.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were several significant things that had happened and one of them was the accident that the Chief of Staff Ramiz Becirovic had. There was an air crash and we were told by the BSA in a meeting that they called us through Colonel Vukovic that there was a crash, and later on, when we investigated, we found that it's true, there was an incident and Ramiz Becirovic, who was the Chief of Staff, was injured. And also we were being told about the rumour of Naser Oric being around and that he was confusing the leadership of the whole ABiH. So I think they were weak at that particular moment, in that there was no proper leadership.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to paragraph 18, which is on the following page, and this discusses shelling in Srebrenica from July 6 until the town fell. Was there any pattern to the shelling that you observed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we noted a pattern that was there --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Suggestive, leading. This witness is eloquent as it is, why lead him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West just referred to the paragraph 18 which refers to a pattern. I don't think it's a leading question. Please proceed. Do you remember the question, Colonel Kingori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. Your Honour, we had noted a pattern in that the BSA could shell over a certain period, then stop, and later on after a few moments start shelling again. And we found that to be a bit interesting. To us it was advantage, yes, in that there was a time that we could go into the town, do crater analysis, and come back safely, also collect those who were injured and those who had been killed and take them to hospital. And also get time to inform the locals that they should stay indoors and not get out so that they can not be harmed. So the pattern was there and we utilised it positively.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, what date did you leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we left I think on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And after the 9th, did the shelling continue in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The shelling continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, while in Potocari we could be able to hear the shells landing and also overflying our place and especially the rockets, at least we knew where the rocket-launcher was, it was just next to Potocari. And secondly, we had our own interpreter whom we had sent to Srebrenica to go and monitor what is happening -- what was happening in that area. So he could also give us the reports of what was happening in Srebrenica and the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to move to paragraph 25, it's the following page. And this is talking about July 11th in the compound itself. On the 11th that's where you were located; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And by the end of the day on the 11th, can you give an estimate about how many people converged in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, around that time we had about from about 3.000 to 3.500. The figure obviously may not be very correct but around that figure had already streamed into Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And does that include the number of the people on the outside of the compound as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Those were the people who were walking in -- into the factory. There were others who had to be kept outside because the factory could not be able to hold everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you know, do you have an estimation of how many people were on the outside of the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, we had a figure of between 5 and 7 outside, but there were estimates which were going up to 10.000 depending on the kind of people who were doing the estimates. Because we had the UNHCR doing it, we had the IOM, we had other agencies who were doing it, but we knew the figure to have been about between 5.000 and 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, at the end of this paragraph you had indicated that there was a massive refugee problem to deal with. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what it was that made you come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, DutchBat -- one thing I can say is that DutchBat was the main supplier of our food and water and even diesel. So there already were strains because they were not being allowed to bring in these items into the enclave by the BSA, they were not giving them a clearance to bring it in. And so when you bring in refugees, when you add refugees now to this problem you find it was very difficult to manage. It was a humanitarian catastrophe in that we did not have enough water, we did not have enough food and even shelter for these refugees in that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell us who Petar was?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Petar was our interpreter from the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how often did you work with him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, Petar -- we used to call him whenever we needed him or whenever he wanted to convey something to us like maybe a request for a meeting with the BSA. And because he had a radio, a UN radio, we could easily communicate. So it was whenever there was a need.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you speak to Petar in the late morning of July 11th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And who called whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: In the morning I -- Your Honour, he's the one who called us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: He was requesting for a meeting with the CO of DutchBat that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the time we were -- we -- a request for an air-strike had already been given to the UN headquarters, and we were expecting air-strikes any time. So we got advice from UN headquarters in Zagreb that we should not attend that meeting because the UN personnel may be held hostage as a human shield to avert an air-strike.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, later in the day did you speak to Petar again?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We talked to Petar. That was -- actually, the air-strike had already been done if you can call that an air-strike because only one aircraft attacked and very few -- there were only two targets which were hit. So everything was over and that time we requested for a meeting, and we were not that afraid because there were no more air-strikes and we had not heard of any threats from the BSA up to that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And ultimately was a meeting held?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to paragraph 27, which starts at the bottom of this same page, and it notes that: "All the trucks and buses were arranged by General Mladic and it was clear that everything was planned including the evacuation. Mladic made a very good show for the BSA TV cameras ..." Colonel, what facts did you consider when you concluded here that everything was planned?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we told General Mladic - and I remember personally once talking to him about it - that the UN will provide transport to take the refugees out of the enclave. And then he declined and said that he had his own buses to take the people outside the enclave. And within a very short time the buses were there. So to me, I could see that because the buses were not being sought from the Yellow Bridge or Bratunac which were the next towns, obviously this is something which had been prearranged. And considering the number of buses and trucks, that could have been a very big logistical issue so it must have been preplanned according to my own assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned that you had this conversation with Mladic. Was there also a second separate conversation with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was a second time that I talked to General Mladic, and that was concerning the people -- the men who had been taken to one white house, where they were put together. And to me it looked very sad because they were all huddled in one particular place and there were too many of them for that particular area. So I thought the conditions therein were not good for them and I wanted him to do something about it. That's when I talked to him a second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When the two of you had the conversation, was it near the white house itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It was not very near the white house but it was not very far because that time it was slightly towards where the refugees were outside -- in the outside compound. But he offered to take me to the -- to that white house so that we could see the conditions. He was still insisting that the conditions were good, that the people were happy inside there, and so he offered to take me there and later on we went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened when you went there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we went to the white house we found the men were still cramped together, there was no space for them to do anything, but then General Mladic offered to, you know, to supply them with candies, soft drinks, beers, and for sure it looked very real, it looked like they were very happy because everybody was scrambling to get something. So they were shouting, "Give me this," "Give me that," and they all looked like they're okay. But to me it was just for the cameras. It was just acting for the cameras to depict that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, ultimately did you ever get inside the white house?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Mladic denied me access to the white house. I asked him for it. I asked him whether he can let me go in there and he said no, I'm not allowed to go inside there, so I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 65 ter 19423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4165, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, you -- early on today you described your role as a military observer and, if I may, as some sort of liaison between the parties. With whom on the VRS side did you primarily meet?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were primarily meeting Major Nikolic who was the main contact guy and also Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how many times did you meet with Colonel Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I met Colonel Vukovic at least four times, at least four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on one of those occasions did take place at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, one of those occasions we met at Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was just one of, you know, like any other meeting, but this one was a bit different, later on we learnt, in that there was something he wanted to convey to us and also there were very many senior officers from his side, from the BSA side, that is, there were about six of them. And one of the questions that he posed to us is what the UN might do in case the BSA attacked the enclave, attacked and took the enclave. He wanted to hear from us what the UN would do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, can you remember when this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it took place quite early, quite early, just before the attack. I think it was around June, around June.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to show you now some video footage, and this is 65 ter 4582, the first part is part 2 of that video, and for the record that's V0009035. In total we'll only play about five minutes. Colonel, this is a July 12th. It's about 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for the Trial Chamber, during the testimony of Colonel Rutten you saw up to this point of where this video starts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And for the record, we've stopped at time 25 and 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, is that you in the middle of the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, right now I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please wait till our usher assists you, Mr. Kingori. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, would you like the witness to view the video again?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, if we could start again. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, I was told that the Colonel watched the video but -- is it true? Can you confirm that you watched the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I've watched it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We can carry on then. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President. If we can -- we are now at 23.59. We are beginning the video. On the screen we see July 12th at 13.13 in the afternoon. Now we can start.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, we just stopped at 24.39. Do you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this an area in which you spent some time that particular day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was there, moving around and checking the situation the whole day, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the people we've seen on the screen, so presently in the minutes earlier, do you recognise some of these people who were there that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. These are people we were with.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now we've stopped at 25.20 and this is a frame of General Mladic speaking to the crowds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: While he was speaking to the crowds, did you remain in the general area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was there throughout and I could see him. We were with him around that area. And he was visibly -- you know, he was present throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were you able to see the reaction of the crowds to his words?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They were very happy. They were assured that everything would be okay. So there was no cause for panic, which is normal in any military operation. You've got to assure the people -- that everything is okay to win their hearts and minds so that they can be on your side. This is normal. Whatever he was doing was what an ordinary leader would do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now we've stopped at 28.59 and where we've stopped, for the record, it was showing a crowd of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, you mentioned earlier that this was part of winning their hearts and minds. Considering your experience, why do you think that this was normal?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is what we call psychological warfare in that you don't want the multitude to rise against you because of what has happened to them. So you want to reassure them, you want to show them that everything is okay, you are taking care of them, and that you ensure nobody is hurt, nobody is harmed. Everybody will go to where they should go to. So it's just to reassure them, though mainly you don't necessarily have to mean what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm going to show you one more video.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this video is just a total of 8 minutes long. It's part of 65 ter 40582. This is part 3. For the record, it's 9016 of that 65 ter number, and we're going to begin at 2 minutes and 44 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've stopped at 3 minutes and 55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, do these events on the video look familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they do, in that I was there during this period and that these people were being led into boarding the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've stopped at 6 minutes and 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person in the middle of the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This was one of the few men from the BSA side who could speak English.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to talk with him during that day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was conveying some messages through him to the higher echelon, the leadership of the BSA that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's 7 minutes and 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We have seen that this road continues on. To where does it go?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: This is a road that leads to Bratunac from Potocari and all the way up from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 7 minutes and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you see yourself in this frame?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you remember being in this area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 8 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if you can tell, you're in this screen and you seem to be coming up behind someone. Do you recognise that person in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: It doesn't look very clear, but I think it was Krstic. [Overlapping speakers] -- remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. What were you trying to do while you were in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was looking for any possible means of telling the leadership, that is, the military leadership of the BSA, that what was happening was not right and especially where the men who were being put in one big house -- in one small house, many of them there, and without any air, without food, without water, without anything. I just wanted to convey that message through somebody.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to continue on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're at 8 minutes and 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, you were just mentioning a place that was too crowded. What was that place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, here I'm referring to the white house where all the men had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're at 9 minutes and 54 seconds. What is this you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, what you can see here is the belongings of the men, that is, the Muslim men who had been taken to the white house, because they were being forced to leave all these belongings outside the house. These belongings included the clothes that they had, that they were carrying, the identity cards, that is, the pass, they could leave the pass there, the identity cards, everything that they had they had to leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue, Mr. President. We only have one more minute of this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to stop at 10 minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Earlier I asked you to identify a person and you mentioned that it was sort of fuzzy. Unfortunately this is kind of fuzzy as well. I know this was a long time ago, but can you identify the person who is standing sort of directly in front of you, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is not very clear. I can't remember him very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember what you were talking about here?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, even here we were just discussing about the general humanitarian situation in that place but through this guy with a blue flak jacket who actually could be able to interpret from English to Serbian language and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll continue now to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is that same footage but it's the Serbian -- version they played on Serbian television. It will continue for a few more seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, what we see at the screen at 10 minutes and 53 seconds, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do recognise this. And as you can see very clearly, this is the upper floor of the house where the men had been taken after being separated from the women and children. And you can see there's no space. They don't have any space at all. And this was the same even in the ground floor, the floor below this, it was the same very bad condition.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you had that discussion with General Mladic, was this the vicinity in which you were standing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is was what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. West. We'll adjourn for today, and Mr. Karadzic will start his cross-examination tomorrow at 9.00. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of January, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.07 p.m.,
